extracted.intended_audience: teachers, teacher-educators, educational policymakers, and students of education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing classroom methods and school conditions that cultivate reflective, inquiry-based thinking rather than rote memorization; covers the features of reflective experience and practical essentials for instruction. Applicable to curriculum design, lesson planning, and teacher practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinking as inquiry (tentative, risky, original)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking is a process of inquiry: seeking, conjecturing, and venturing into the unknown; conclusions are tentative or hypothetical and involve risk rather than dogmatic assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all classroom thinking as 'original research' for the thinker; accept uncertainty and probabilistic inference (e.g., the eclipse/astronomer example). Encourage conjectures that guide action and recognize that conclusions must be tested by consequences and events. Anti-patterns: presenting thought as fixed facts or encouraging dogmatic final assertions without testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a genuine empirical situation as the initiator of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial stage of thinking is experience: pupils must have an actual empirical situation (trying to do something and noting its consequences) to begin thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin lessons with a doing/task situation similar to everyday life (play, work, experiments) rather than starting with abstract ready-made material. Example: child building with blocks; scientist experimenting with unfamiliar objects. Anti-patterns: beginning instruction with isolated abstractions or expecting thought to be cultivated in isolation from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure problems are genuine, not simulated or mock
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems presented to pupils should naturally arise from a situation or personal experience and be the pupil's own problem rather than a teacher/textbook contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two diagnostic questions from the text: (a) Does the question naturally suggest itself within some situation or personal experience? (b) Is it the pupil's own problem or merely the teacher's/textbook's imposed task? Avoid problems that exist only to test recall, win marks, or satisfy external requirements. Anti-patterns: artificial 'problems' whose only purpose is examination performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient and appropriate data/resources to think with
rubrics_metrics.description: Pupils must possess or have access to facts, observations, experiences, and other resources needed to cope with the difficulty at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance use of memory, observation, reading, and communication depending on the problem. Avoid assuming students can 'spin solutions out of their heads' with no material base. Do not over-rely on sense-presentations when recall suffices, nor over-rely on others (books/teachers) to supply ready-made solutions. Ensure the teacher supplies usable material rather than finished answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster pupil-generated suggestions, inferences, and tentative explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking requires projection, invention, and conjecture: pupils should produce tentative hypotheses and imaginative use of familiar materials in new contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage creative recombination of familiar elements (Newton example). Value originality as novel operations, not fanciful materials. Teachers should prompt and hold pupils responsible for developing their own suggested solutions in orderly ways. Anti-patterns: supplying the idea/solution directly so the pupil never invents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test ideas by application (active experimental testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas and hypotheses must be applied and tested by acting upon them; application converts tentative thoughts into meaningful, validated knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities (experiments, projects, expeditions) where students' hypotheses guide action and consequences reveal validity. Emphasize that thinking remains suspended until tested. Anti-patterns: confining 'application' to rote practice that only fixes previously learned material without intellectual testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match problem difficulty to prior experience (challenge with familiar 'luminous spots')
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should be novel enough to provoke thought yet sufficiently connected to previous habits so pupils have points of contact for solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make difficulties large enough to challenge but small enough to allow pupils to use familiar resources; avoid overwhelming puzzles that discourage thinking and avoid trivial tasks that do not require inference. Teachers should craft tasks with a mix of novel and familiar elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating information as an end (use information as working capital)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge/information should function as the working capital for inquiry, not as a static end to be heaped up for reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning so information is acquired for application in problem-solving, not mere recitation. Beware of curricula that reward accumulation for examinations. Anti-patterns: emphasizing storage and display of facts divorced from use, producing a 'mind cluttered with miscellaneous junk'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide materials, appliances, and active pursuits that reproduce life situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools should supply labs, shops, gardens, dramatizations, plays, games, and other material opportunities that generate real problems and occasions for thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, use manual/constructive activities for intellectual purposes (not merely physical skill or pecuniary ends). If full facilities aren't available, teachers must still seek or simulate active pursuits in class. Anti-patterns: classroom setups focused solely on listening, reading, and rote repetition; lack of 'stuff' to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher as participant and co-learner (conjoint experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher should take a sympathetic, participating role—sharing in activity with pupils rather than merely furnishing ready-made ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In shared activity the teacher also learns; the less consciousness of 'giving' or 'receiving' instruction the better. Participation involves guiding, supplying materials, and collaborating in inquiry rather than lecturing finished answers. Anti-patterns: teacher standing off, supplying solutions, or treating pupils as passive recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate habits of selecting and using appropriate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must develop the ability to select what information is appropriate for solving problems rather than having everything treated on a single static level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide repeated practice in choosing relevant facts from stored material; design exercises where pupils must search past experiences or readings for resources. Anti-patterns: indiscriminate accumulation with no practice in selection, leading to inability to deploy knowledge in new contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application exercises must retain intellectual quality (not only skill-fixing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice in applying learned material should primarily exercise intellectual judgment, not merely physical or mechanical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame application tasks to test ideas and deepen understanding (use application to reveal meaning and validity), not solely to increase speed or dexterity. Anti-patterns: treating laboratory/shop work solely as vocational training or repetitive skill practice without reflective aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unify instruction across lessons and subjects (continuity of experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction is more educative when lessons are interconnected: students should habitually use earlier lessons to understand current ones and use current lessons to illuminate earlier material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating each lesson as an independent whole. Promote systematic linking between lessons and subjects; encourage students to find points of contact and mutual bearings. Anti-patterns: isolated lessons that leave out-of-school experience unanalyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage pupil ownership of problems (personal relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should be the pupil's own—connected to their interests and life—rather than problems whose primary aim is satisfying school conventions or approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that are meaningful beyond grades: foster curiosity as it appears outside school. Anti-patterns: problems posed only to 'get a required mark' or to comply with external standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the phases/features of reflective experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A reflective experience includes (i) perplexity/doubt about an indeterminate situation; (ii) a tentative conjectural anticipation; (iii) careful survey/analysis of attainable considerations; (iv) elaboration of the hypothesis for precision and consistency; (v) taking a stand and testing by action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure lessons and activities to elicit and practice these five stages explicitly: present problematic situations, guide hypothesis formation, teach systematic examination, encourage orderly elaboration, and provide means for experimental testing. Use this sequence as a checklist for lesson design and assessment.
